title: The Missing
full_review:
�����������When a film opens with a character being instructed to recite the 23rd Psalm -- "The Lord is my shepherd" -- viewers know they are in for some dark valleys ahead. It doesn't get much darker than "The Missing" (Columbia), Ron Howard's scenically eloquent but quite violent Western about a frontier mother racing against time and hope to rescue her daughter from a band of ruthless desperadoes headed by an evil Indian shaman.

Despite emotionally complex performances and breathtaking vistas, Howard's oater remains a fundamentally bleak experience -- a misguided attempt to prove his maturation as a filmmaker by indulging in abrasive onscreen ugliness.

Set in 1885, the story revolves around Maggie Gilkeson (Cate Blanchett), a strong-willed homesteader/healer raising two daughters -- teenage Lily (Evan Rachel Wood) and younger sister Dot (Jenna Boyd) -- in the New Mexico Territory. Being a "God-fearin' Christian," however, doesn't preclude her from jumping into the saddle with her live-in, cowpoke boyfriend Brake (Aaron Eckhart) after the girls are put to bed.

But Maggie's little life on the prairie is disrupted by the unwelcome return of her estranged father, Samuel (Tommy Lee Jones), who abandoned his family when she was a child to live among the Apache, adopting their ways. When he informs her that he requires medical attention, Maggie responds with uncharacteristic, though understandable, coldness -- tearing into him about the devastating toll his desertion had on her mother and disgusted by his "goin' Injun." After a rough examination of his injury, she asks him to leave and never return.

However, when Lily is brutally abducted by Pesh-Chidin (Eric Schweig), a Native American "brujo" -- or witch doctor -- Maggie is left with no option but to turn to Samuel for help. Along with the spunky Dot, Maggie and Samuel struggle to track down the mixed-race band of outlaws before they can cross the border into Mexico where Lily and several other women kidnapped by Pesh-Chidin will be sold into slavery. The trail is rife with danger -- including a flash flood in a gorge that nearly sweeps Dot away. Though skilled at navigating the rugged landscape, Samuel proves far less adept at piloting the emotional terrain of Maggie's bitterness and mistrust.

Borrowing heavily from John Ford's "The Searchers" (1956), "The Missing" offers some of the most stunning big-sky cinematography in recent memory. Beautiful visuals aside, the story would have been better served if Howard had scalped about a half-hour off its 130-minute running time -- especially as the narrative progresses into more conventional action territory. And while the film effectively captures the daily hardships of frontier life, viewers must contend with a steady stream of gratuitous brutality, including several gunfights, people shot with bows and arrows or bludgeoned with cudgels and various victims of Pesh-Chidin's black magic.

Rather than subscribe to oversimplified ethnic stereotypes which either demonize Indians as savages (as in most classic Westerns) or portray them as eco-friendly pacifists (as in "Dances With Wolves"), the film shows Native Americans to be capable of both acts of selfless heroism and barbarous cruelty. Howard also avoids simplistic Indian-good/white-man-bad dichotomies, meting out vice and virtue in equal measure.

Regrettably, Howard employs a view of religion which fuses Christianity and Native American shamanism into a syncretic stew. Several scenes may raise red flags for Catholic viewers, including one in which Samuel "heals" Maggie of a hex placed on her by Pesh-Chidin by reciting Native American incantations over her fevered body. In another, he instructs her and Dot to wear special beaded necklaces as protection against the brujo's sorcery -- as if they provide a stronger defense against evil than does her Christian faith.

Despite their period look, the characters are informed by a distinctly modern attitude toward religion. Maggie is typical of contemporary believers who tend to define religion as either private spirituality (she is seen praying the psalms throughout) or social justice (she helps those in need), but whose faith holds little sway over personal piety, especially when it comes to sexual morality (she has a child out of wedlock and lives with a man who is not her husband).

Nevertheless, at its core "The Missing" is a well-carpentered tale about forgiveness and redemption through self-sacrifice; for this, it is worth recommending, but not without, er, reservations.

Due to recurring graphic violence, an implied sexual encounter, a suicide, as well as sporadic crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
